If a creature has deathtouch, any amount of damage it deals to a creature is considered lethal damage for the purpose of determining excess damage. This means that if a creature with both trample and deathtouch is blocked, its controller only needs to assign 1 damage to each blocking creature to satisfy the lethal damage requirement, and the rest of the damage can be assigned to the defending player or planeswalker. results.question: can you explain layers?
results.text: The layer system is a method used in Magic: The Gathering to determine the order in which continuous effects are applied to objects. Continuous effects are those that are active continuously, not just for a moment. The game applies these effects in a series of layers and sublayers, ensuring that characteristics of objects are consistently determined. The process begins with the object's base characteristics, whether printed on a card or defined by an effect that created it [613.1]. Then, continuous effects are applied in a specific order of layers [613.1]. These layers include, but are not limited to, Layer 1 (rules and effects that modify copiable values, including copy effects and effects from merging with permanents) [613.1a, 613.2a], Layer 3 (text-changing effects) [613.1c], Layer 4 (type-changing effects) [613.1d], Layer 5 (color-changing effects) [613.1e], and Layer 7 (power and toughness changing effects, which has its own sublayers) [613.4]. Within each layer or sublayer, effects are typically applied in timestamp order, meaning earlier effects are applied before later ones [613.7]. However, dependency can alter this order [613.8]. If an effect applies to multiple layers, its parts are applied in their respective layers, and the effect continues to apply to the same objects even if the source of the effect is removed [613.6].

results.question: My opponent's [Grizzly Bears] has 2 damage marked on it. Do state-based actions make it die before my [Lightning Bolt] resolves?
results.text: No, state-based actions do not make your opponent's Grizzly Bears die before your Lightning Bolt resolves. Lightning Bolt is an instant spell, and instants can be cast when a player has priority. State-based actions are checked only when a player would receive priority, or when an effect that ends the turn or combat phase occurs. Since Lightning Bolt is being cast, it will go on the stack, and then resolve before state-based actions are checked. After Lightning Bolt resolves and deals 3 damage to Grizzly Bears, the damage is marked on it. Then, state-based actions will be checked. Grizzly Bears has 2 damage marked on it, and its toughness is 2. Since the damage marked on it is not greater than or equal to its toughness, it will not be destroyed by state-based actions. If the damage had been lethal, it would have been destroyed as a state-based action after Lightning Bolt resolved, but before you would have received priority again.

results.question: It's my upkeep. My [Phyrexian Arena]'s beginning-of-upkeep trigger and my opponent's own beginning-of-upkeep trigger both want to go on the stack. Who chooses the order, and when exactly do they trigger?
results.text: When your upkeep step begins, both your Phyrexian Arena's triggered ability and your opponent's triggered ability trigger simultaneously because they both trigger "at the beginning of" the upkeep step [500.6]. These abilities are put onto the stack before either player receives priority [117.3a]. Since you are the active player, you will put your triggered ability on the stack first, and then your opponent will put their triggered ability on the stack [101.4]. This means your opponent's ability will resolve before yours [603.3b].

results.question: I cast a sorcery with buyback and pay its buyback cost, then copy that spell with [Fork]. Once everything resolves, how many copies of the card end up back in my hand?
results.text: No copies of the card will end up back in your hand. When you cast the sorcery with buyback and pay its buyback cost, the spell will be put into your hand instead of your graveyard as it resolves [702.27a]. When Fork copies the spell, the copy is not cast and does not have a card associated with it [707.10, Fork ruling #9]. Therefore, the copy of the spell cannot have its buyback cost paid, and it will not return to your hand [Fork ruling #8]. The original sorcery, having resolved and been put into your hand, is not affected by the copy.

results.question: I have a face-down manifested card that's really [Lightning Bolt]. It dies and I imprint it on [Mimic Vat]. Later I activate Mimic Vat's copy ability -- do I get a token?
results.text: No, you do not get a token. Although you can imprint a manifested card onto Mimic Vat, a manifested card is not a creature, and Mimic Vat's triggered ability only exiles nontoken creatures [Mimic Vat ruling #0]. Therefore, even though you attempted to imprint Lightning Bolt, it would not have been exiled by Mimic Vat's triggered ability. Since no card is exiled with Mimic Vat, no token can be created when you activate its copy ability [Mimic Vat ruling #6].

results.question: My [Fiend Hunter]'s enters-the-battlefield ability is on the stack, about to exile a creature. I copy that ability with [Lithoform Engine] and target a second creature. Both get exiled. When Fiend Hunter later leaves the battlefield, do both come back?
results.text: Yes, both creatures exiled by Fiend Hunter's abilities will return to the battlefield when Fiend Hunter leaves the battlefield. The Lithoform Engine's ability creates a copy of Fiend Hunter's enters-the-battlefield ability. This copied ability also exiles a creature. According to the rulings for Lithoform Engine, if an ability is linked to a second ability, copies of that first ability are also linked to that second ability. In this case, Fiend Hunter's second ability, which returns the exiled card to the battlefield under its owner's control when Fiend Hunter leaves the battlefield, is linked to its first ability. Therefore, when Fiend Hunter leaves the battlefield, both the creature exiled by the original ability and the creature exiled by the copied ability will be returned to the battlefield. This is because the second ability refers to all cards exiled by the first ability and its copy. [Lithoform Engine ruling #4]

results.question: My own [Banishing Light] has an opponent's creature exiled. On my opponent's turn I cast [Teferi's Protection], phasing out my Banishing Light. Does the exiled creature return to the battlefield?
results.text: No, the exiled creature does not return to the battlefield. Teferi's Protection causes your permanents, including Banishing Light, to phase out. When Banishing Light phases out, it is treated as though it doesn't exist [702.26c]. Because Banishing Light is phased out, the effect that exiles the creature, which lasts "until this enchantment leaves the battlefield," does not end. Therefore, the creature remains exiled [702.26f]. Additionally, Teferi's Protection ruling #21 states that one-shot effects waiting "until [this] leaves the battlefield" do not happen when a permanent phases out.

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. In response to its cast trigger, my opponent tries to [Counterspell] it. Can they even target it given protection from instants, and if it's countered, do I still control their next turn?
results.text: No, your opponent cannot target Emrakul, the Promised End with Counterspell. Emrakul, the Promised End has "protection from instants" [702.16b]. This means it cannot be targeted by spells with the quality "instant" [702.16b]. Even though Emrakul, the Promised End has protection from instants, its abilities that trigger when you cast it function while it is on the stack [113.6g]. If Emrakul, the Promised End were countered, the effect that causes you to control your opponent during their next turn would not happen because the spell would not resolve [608.2b]. If Emrakul, the Promised End resolves, you will control your opponent during their next turn, and they will take an extra turn after that [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14].

results.question: My cascade spell exiles cards until it hits [Valki, God of Lies], whose back face is the seven-mana planeswalker Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor. Is that a legal cascade hit, and can I cast the Tibalt side for free?
results.text: Yes, Valki, God of Lies is a legal cascade hit, but you cannot cast the Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor side for free. Cascade exiles cards until a nonland card with a mana value less than the cascade spell's mana value is found [702.85a]. Valki, God of Lies has a mana cost of {1}{B}, giving it a mana value of 2 [712.8e]. If your cascade spell has a mana value greater than 2, Valki, God of Lies would be a legal hit. However, the cascade ability allows you to cast the exiled card without paying its mana cost only if the resulting spell's mana value is less than the cascade spell's mana value [702.85a]. The Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor face has a mana cost of {5}{B}{R}, giving it a mana value of 7 [Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #16]. Since the mana value of Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor (7) is not less than the mana value of Valki, God of Lies (2), you cannot cast Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor for free. Furthermore, when casting a modal double-faced card, only the characteristics of the face you are casting are considered [Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #14]. Therefore, if you were to cast Valki, God of Lies, you would be casting its front face, Valki, God of Lies, not Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor.
citations: Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #16
Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #14

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. With its cast trigger on the stack, I copy that trigger with [Lithoform Engine]. Then I untap Lithoform Engine with [Voltaic Key] and use it again to copy [Emrakul, the Promised End] itself as a permanent spell. How many of my opponent's turns do I control, do I get a second Emrakul, and does copying the Emrakul spell give me another control-a-turn trigger?
results.text: You will control your opponent's next turn, and then that opponent will take an extra turn after that. You will not get a second Emrakul, the Promised End, and copying the Emrakul spell will not give you another control-a-turn trigger. The cast trigger of Emrakul, the Promised End creates two effects: one that grants you control of target opponent during that player's next turn, and one that gives that player an extra turn after that. When you copy the cast trigger with Lithoform Engine, you create a second instance of both of these effects. The last player-controlling effect to be created is the one that works, so the first Emrakul, the Promised End's effect will control your opponent's next turn, and the second, copied effect will grant them an extra turn after that. The second ability of Emrakul, the Promised End, which grants control of an opponent's turn, is a triggered ability that triggers when you cast Emrakul, the Promised End. Copying the spell itself with Lithoform Engine does not cause this triggered ability to trigger again, as a copy of a spell is not cast [707.10d].

results.question: I've imprinted a creature on [Mimic Vat] and activate its ability to make a token copy. While that ability is on the stack, I copy it with [Lithoform Engine]. Do I get two tokens?
results.text: Yes, you will get two tokens. When you activate Mimic Vat's ability, it goes on the stack. Then, you use Lithoform Engine's ability to copy that activated ability. This results in two instances of the Mimic Vat ability on the stack. When the first instance resolves, it creates a token that is a copy of the card exiled with Mimic Vat. When the second instance resolves, it creates another token that is a copy of the card exiled with Mimic Vat. The token created by a copy of a spell or ability copies both the characteristics of the spell or ability and all decisions made for it, including targets [707.10b, 707.2a]. The ability of Lithoform Engine states that you may choose new targets for the copy, but this is not applicable here as Mimic Vat's ability does not have targets [Lithoform Engine ruling #3]. The token created by a resolving copy of a spell becomes a token when it resolves, and it is not said to have been "created" for the purposes of replacement effects or triggered abilities that refer to creating a token [111.13, Lithoform Engine ruling #15]. However, this does not affect the creation of the tokens themselves.

results.question: An opponent controls an untapped [Trinisphere], and I have a permanent that makes my green spells cost {1} less. I want to cast [Awaken the Woods] for value. If I cast it with X=0, what does it cost and what do I get, and what X should I actually choose?
results.text: If you cast Awaken the Woods with X=0 while your opponent controls an untapped Trinisphere and you have a permanent that makes your green spells cost {1} less, the total cost to cast Awaken the Woods will be {2}{G}. You will create zero 1/1 green Forest Dryad land creature tokens. To cast Awaken the Woods for its awaken ability, you should choose X=3. If you cast Awaken the Woods with X=3, the mana cost is {3}{G}{G}. Your permanent reduces the cost by {1}, making the cost {2}{G}{G}. Trinisphere then applies, increasing the cost to {3}{G}{G} because the mana component of the cost ({2}{G}{G}) is less than three mana. You will create three 1/1 green Forest Dryad land creature tokens. The awaken ability itself requires paying the awaken cost, which is {X}{G}{G} [702.113a]. If you choose to pay the awaken cost, you would pay {3}{G}{G} for X=3, and then Trinisphere would apply to that cost. However, the question asks about casting Awaken the Woods for value, implying the use of its awaken ability. The awaken ability is a spell ability that is part of the spell itself [702.113a]. When casting a spell with an {X} in its mana cost, the controller chooses the value of X as part of casting the spell [107.3a]. The mana value of Awaken the Woods is 2, regardless of the value of X [202.3e]. When casting Awaken the Woods with X=0, the mana cost is {0}{G}{G}. Your permanent reduces this to {G}{G}. Trinisphere then applies, increasing the cost to {3} because the mana component of the cost ({G}{G}) is less than three mana. The total cost becomes {3}. You will create zero 1/1 green Forest Dryad land creature tokens [702.113a]. To get the most value from Awaken the Woods, you should choose X=3. The mana cost is {3}{G}{G}. Your permanent reduces this to {2}{G}{G}. Trinisphere then applies, increasing the cost to {3}{G}{G} because the mana component of the cost ({2}{G}{G}) is less than three mana. The total cost is {3}{G}{G}. You will create three 1/1 green Forest Dryad land creature tokens [702.113a].

results.question: [Grist, the Hunger Tide] is in my graveyard. Can I return it with [Animate Dead], and what happens?
results.text: Yes, you can return Grist, the Hunger Tide from your graveyard to the battlefield with Animate Dead. When Animate Dead enters the battlefield, it will return Grist, the Hunger Tide to the battlefield under your control. Because Grist, the Hunger Tide is on the battlefield, it will no longer be a creature and will be just a planeswalker. Animate Dead will then attach to Grist, the Hunger Tide. If Animate Dead leaves the battlefield, Grist, the Hunger Tide's controller will sacrifice it. This is because Grist, the Hunger Tide is a creature card in the graveyard when targeted by Animate Dead, and Animate Dead's effect returns it to the battlefield. [Animate Dead ruling #1]

results.question: My commander [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] has four +1/+1 counters on it. It dies, I move it to the command zone, then recast it. Does it keep the counters, and does [Doubling Season] double them as it re-enters?
results.text: Skullbriar, the Walking Grave does not keep its counters when it moves to the command zone. When Skullbriar, the Walking Grave dies, it moves to the graveyard. Counters on an object are not retained if that object moves from one zone to another [122.2]. The counters are not "removed"; they simply cease to exist [122.2]. When Skullbriar, the Walking Grave is recast from the command zone, it enters the battlefield as a new object [400.7]. If Doubling Season is on the battlefield when Skullbriar, the Walking Grave re-enters, it will enter with double the normal number of +1/+1 counters, as Doubling Season affects permanents that enter with counters [Doubling Season ruling #2]. However, Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's own ability states that counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library. This ability overrides the general rule [122.2] that counters are lost when moving zones. Therefore, if Skullbriar, the Walking Grave dies and is moved to the command zone, it will not retain its counters. When it is recast, it will enter with the base number of counters determined by Doubling Season, if applicable, and not the counters it had previously.

results.question: I cast [Final Fortune] to take an extra turn. During that extra turn I use [Sundial of the Infinite] to end the turn before the end step. Do I still lose the game?
results.text: No, you do not lose the game. When you activate Sundial of the Infinite's ability during your extra turn, it ends the turn before the end step is reached. Since the end step is skipped, the triggered ability that causes you to lose the game at the beginning of that turn's end step does not trigger. This is because the game skips straight to the cleanup step, and "at the beginning of the end step" triggered abilities do not trigger if the end step is skipped [724.1e]. The ruling for Final Fortune also states that if you skip the extra turn gained, you do not lose the game [Final Fortune ruling #1].

results.question: I cast [Clone]. When and how do I choose what it copies, and can my opponent respond to that choice?
results.text: You choose what Clone copies as it enters the battlefield. This choice is part of the process of Clone entering the battlefield, not a separate event. Your opponent can respond to Clone entering the battlefield, but they cannot respond to the choice of what Clone copies because that choice is made as it enters the battlefield, which is a single event. The ability of Clone that allows you to choose a creature to copy is a replacement effect that modifies how Clone enters the battlefield [Clone ruling #2]. This choice is made when Clone is entering the battlefield, and it is not a spell or ability that can be responded to. Your opponent can respond to the casting of Clone, or to abilities that trigger when Clone enters the battlefield, but not to the choice of what Clone copies.

results.question: I activate my [Flooded Strand]'s ability, then activate [Gogo, Master of Mimicry] with X=2 to copy it twice. How many lands do I get from that one Flooded Strand?
results.text: You will get one land from activating Flooded Strand. Gogo, Master of Mimicry's ability copies activated or triggered abilities that are on the stack [Gogo, Master of Mimicry ruling #6]. The ability of Flooded Strand is an activated ability that, when activated, searches your library for a Plains or Island card and puts it onto the battlefield. When Gogo, Master of Mimicry copies this ability, it creates additional instances of that ability on the stack [Gogo, Master of Mimicry ruling #6]. However, the ability of Flooded Strand does not create any lands; it searches for a land and puts it onto the battlefield. Therefore, even with the copies, you only get one land from the original Flooded Strand activation.
